title: Sophocles, Hesiod, Euripides (18 tragedies), and Aeschylus
shelf_note: A Greek manuscript of the tragedians (Laurenziana); sampled leaves are Sophocles' Electra, Euripides' Bacchae and Medea. Squarely on the classics shelf. The hand looks later than the catalogue date '1350'; not verified.
structure_note: printed_repeats 143 and backsteps 33 fit a foliated manuscript (one folio number per leaf, read on both faces, plus misread numerals) rather than a splice. Page 524 is a correctly marked blank endleaf. 25 pages have no OCR.

book_verdict: A real tragedians manuscript on the right shelf, but the OCR has not read the hand. Lines are invented or garbled, speakers are made up, and on one leaf every line is doubled. The English translates that invented text, and one leaf's translation stops after the first column.
reader_summary: A Byzantine-era manuscript of Sophocles and Euripides (Electra, Bacchae, Medea seen). The transcription is largely not the manuscript's text: lines are reconstructed or garbled, and on page 40 the play is misidentified as Euripides' Orestes. The English cannot be trusted as a translation of these leaves. Only the images are useful.

book_verdict: Correct leaves and a recognisable Proclus text, but every page has meaning-changing misreadings of abbreviations and names. On page 270 a misread turns Proclus' claim about self-refutation into its negation, and the English follows it.
reader_summary: Proclus' commentary on Plato's Alcibiades I in a Renaissance Greek hand. The transcription follows the manuscript line by line and gets most words, but it misexpands abbreviations and sometimes drops or inverts the sense. The English is a usable guide to the argument and should be checked against the Greek (or Westerink's edition) before anyone quotes it.

title: Vitruvii de architectura libri X
shelf_note: A medieval Latin manuscript of Vitruvius (Laurenziana); on the shelf.
structure_note: 18 backsteps and 14 repeats in 116 pages: the leaves carry a modern foliation in the top corner (18, 24, 54), and the OCR misreads some of these (page 24 reads '14' where the leaf shows 18). Page 30 has a large loss at the lower inner corner (the white area is missing parchment, not an overlay). The last leaf (115) is a stained endleaf.

book_verdict: A fine early manuscript of Vitruvius, but the OCR often composes plausible Latin instead of expanding the abbreviations. The English follows it: Socrates becomes 'the father-in-law', and half of page 24 is untranslated.
reader_summary: A medieval Latin copy of Vitruvius, De architectura. The transcription is a partly abbreviated, partly invented reading: some passages are close, others (e.g. Book II on larch and the Apennines) are not the manuscript's text. The English cannot be trusted. A reader should use a printed Vitruvius alongside the images.
